text:
A clearer path from finding a home
to starting a conversation.
Project presentation  |  Full stack web application

RentBridge is a rental marketplace built with a React frontend, Express API, and MongoDB persistence. This presentation describes current project implementation and separates existing features from proposed enhancements.
A rental marketplace built around the next step
RentBridge brings property discovery, posting, and contact requests into one workflow.

Find a place.
Share a listing.
Start a conversation.
Customers browse and save properties, and can also publish listings. Owners manage listings and respond to interested customers.
Search, filter, view photos and details.
Create a property listing with images.
Send a request and follow its status.
Sources: frontend/src/main.jsx, frontend/src/styles.css, backend/src/routes/properties.js, backend/src/routes/contactRequests.js. Customer accounts can publish property listings as well as browse.
The gap is between discovery and trusted contact
Design challenge framed from the product workflow, not a measured market claim.

People need enough clarity to decide whether to reach out,
then a simple way to track what happens next.
Photos, pricing, location, and property details need to be easy to scan together.
A customer should be able to express interest without exposing private details up front.
Both sides need a clear signal when a request is sent and when it is accepted or declined.
Problem statement is a design challenge inferred from app features and workflow. It does not claim quantified user research or market statistics.
Make the rental journey easier to act on
Product objectives translated into features present in the current build.
Search and review property details in one place.
Let owners and customers publish listings.
Send, accept, or decline contact requests.
Reveal direct contact information after acceptance.
Current implementation references: backend/src/routes/properties.js, backend/src/routes/contactRequests.js, backend/src/routes/notifications.js, and ContactRequest and Notification models.
A simple flow from listing to accepted contact
One account model supports browsing, posting, and responding.

Add property facts
and up to five photos

Customer asks to
contact the poster

Poster accepts or
declines the request
The customer receives an in-app notification with contact details; the listing’s exact address and poster email stay private until then.

Current flow: a customer creates a contact request; the poster accepts or declines. Acceptance sends an in-app notification with contact details and reveals exact address through the authorized request flow.
The browser handles interaction; the API enforces workflow and access; MongoDB stores records.

Responsive interface
Property search and forms
Favorites and notification views

REST routes for auth, listings,
contact requests, notifications
JWT-protected actions

Users, properties, requests,
and notifications
Multer-managed image uploads
Password hashing • role-aware authorization • validated image uploads • CORS and rate limits • persistent storage required for production uploads

Stack checked against frontend/package.json, backend/package.json, backend/src/server.js, backend/src/routes/auth.js, and backend/src/models. Current uploads use local disk; production needs persistent disk or cloud object storage.
How a contact request moves through RentBridge
Editable system view • arrows show user requests and storage flows.
ACCEPTED REQUEST → private notification returns contact details; exact address stays protected until approval.

Data flow reflects the current application architecture: customers and posters use React; Express handles auth, properties, contact requests, and notifications; MongoDB stores users, properties, requests, and notifications; Multer handles images. On approval, private contact information is returned through the authorized notification flow.
Make the next action visible to both sides
Expected user outcomes from the current product design; no impact metrics are claimed.
View photos, rent, and property details.
See when a poster accepts or declines.
Accept or decline a contact request.
Customers can publish listings too; the poster controls each incoming request.
Qualitative user outcomes are derived from current functionality. The app has two account types, owner and customer; customers can upload property listings.
A practical roadmap beyond the current build
Potential next steps to improve reliability, trust, and reach.
Move image uploads to persistent object storage and a CDN.
Add opt-in email or push alerts alongside in-app notifications.
Add listing reports, moderation tools, and review workflows.
Add paginated search, automated end-to-end tests, and shared rate-limit storage.
These are proposed enhancements, not features in the current release.

Future work based on current constraints: uploads are local disk-backed, notifications are in-app, public property results are capped, and rate limiting is process-local. These ideas are not currently implemented.
